outline: 643 Area of Composite Figures with Special Quadrilaterals

examples.solution_text:
The perpendicular height bisects the base, giving a half-base of $10\div2=5\text{ cm}$.

$\begin{aligned}h&=\sqrt{12^{2}-5^{2}}\\&=\sqrt{119}\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}A&=\frac{10\times\sqrt{119}}{2}\\&=5\sqrt{119}\\&\approx54.54\text{ cm}^{2}\end{aligned}$

The horizontal overhang is $23-14=9\text{ cm}$.

$\begin{aligned}h&=\sqrt{15^{2}-9^{2}}\\&=\sqrt{144}\\&=12\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}A&=\frac{12}{2}(14+23)\\&=222\text{ cm}^{2}\end{aligned}$

The overhangs are equal, so each is $(26-14)\div2=6\text{ cm}$.

$\begin{aligned}h&=\sqrt{9^{2}-6^{2}}\\&=\sqrt{45}\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}A&=\frac{\sqrt{45}}{2}(14+26)\\&=20\sqrt{45}\\&\approx134.2\text{ cm}^{2}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}a&=\sqrt{10^{2}-6^{2}}\\&=8\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}b&=\sqrt{15^{2}-6^{2}}\\&=\sqrt{189}\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$

The full horizontal diagonal is $2\times6=12\text{ cm}$. The full vertical diagonal is $(8+\sqrt{189})\text{ cm}$.

$\begin{aligned}A&=\frac{12(8+\sqrt{189})}{2}\\&=48+6\sqrt{189}\text{ cm}^{2}\end{aligned}$

The diagonals bisect each other at right angles. Half the known diagonal is $16\div2=8\text{ cm}$.

$\begin{aligned}m&=\sqrt{17^{2}-8^{2}}\\&=\sqrt{225}\\&=15\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$

The other full diagonal is $2\times15=30\text{ cm}$.

$\begin{aligned}A&=\frac{16\times30}{2}\\&=240\text{ cm}^{2}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}x^{2}+x^{2}&=16^{2}\\2x^{2}&=256\\x^{2}&=128\end{aligned}$

The area is $x^{2}$, so there is no need to find $x$.

$A=128\text{ cm}^{2}$

The perpendicular height bisects the base, so each half is $6\text{ cm}$.

$\begin{aligned}h&=\sqrt{12^{2}-6^{2}}\\&=\sqrt{108}\\&=6\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}A&=\frac{12\times6\sqrt{3}}{2}\\&=36\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}^{2}\end{aligned}$

methods.description: Subtract squares to find a missing shorter side, then use half the product of the perpendicular sides for area; retain exact values when required.
Halve the base, use Pythagoras to find the perpendicular height, then calculate area using the full base; round only the final result.
Find the horizontal overhang from the difference of the parallel sides when necessary, use Pythagoras for height, then apply the trapezium area formula.
Halve the difference of the parallel sides to find each equal overhang, use Pythagoras for height, then apply the trapezium area formula.
Use Pythagoras separately for the two segments of the symmetry diagonal, add them, double the other half-diagonal, then halve the product of the full diagonals.
Use the perpendicular bisecting diagonals and a side to find a missing half-diagonal, double both half-diagonals, then apply the rhombus area formula.
Use equal sides in Pythagoras to obtain the side length squared directly, which is the square’s area.
Bisect the base of an equilateral triangle, find its height using Pythagoras, simplify the surd, then calculate exact area.

examples.derivation: The marked perpendicular sides give h²=8²−5²=39. Thus h=√39 m and A=5√39/2 m².
The half-base is 5 cm. Then h²=12²−5²=119 and A=10√119/2=5√119≈54.54 cm².
The overhang is 23−14=9 cm. Hence h=√(15²−9²)=12 cm and A=12(14+23)/2=222 cm².
Each equal overhang is (26−14)/2=6 cm. Thus h=√(9²−6²)=√45 cm and A=20√45≈134.2 cm².
The perpendicular half-diagonal is 6 cm. Then a=√(10²−6²)=8 cm and b=√(15²−6²)=√189 cm. Full diagonals are 12 cm and (8+√189) cm, giving A=48+6√189 cm².
Half the known diagonal is 8 cm. The other half-diagonal is m=√(17²−8²)=15 cm, so its full length is 30 cm. Therefore A=16×30/2=240 cm².
The square’s diagonal gives x²+x²=16², so 2x²=256 and x²=128. Its area is therefore 128 cm².
The altitude halves the 12 cm base. Thus h=√(12²−6²)=√108=6√3 cm and A=12×6√3/2=36√3 cm².
